newsitem.title: INDIA: Bhutto removal wakes instability fears - newspapers.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto removal wakes instability fears - newspapers.

text.p: The dismissal of Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's government aroused concerns over regional instability in Indian newspapers on Wednesday.
Editorials urged the Indian government not to assume that bilateral relations would automatically improve after the Bhutto government's dismissal by President Farooq Leghari.
Democracy would need time to stabilise, they said.

"...(The Indian government) would be well advised not to automatically assume that a change of guard in Pakistan must necessarily improve bilateral relations," the Hindustan Times, the Indian capital's leading daily, said.

Indian officials on Tuesday reacted calmly to Bhutto's dismissal. Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said it was an internal affair and that India had always been keen to maintain good neighbourly relations.
The Times of India hoped the U.S. would use its influence in the region carefully.

"It is going to take both time and effort to stabilise democracy in Pakistan and U.S. influence on Pakistani politics is one of the determinant factors in the process but has not always been wisely exercised," it said.

The Hindustan Times said U.S. influence might see Pakistan increasing its military assistance to the Taleban militia in neighbouring Afghanistan, which overthrew the government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani late in September.
Rabbani's government has alleged that Pakistan has supported the Islamic Taleban militia.
"The (Pakistani) army-bureaucracy axis may...feel less inhibited by American coolness in significantly increasing military assistance to the Taleban in Kabul," the Hindustan Times said.
It also called for more vigilance in the troubled Himalayan region of Kashmir.
Neighbours India and Pakistan were carved out of British India in 1947 in a blood-stained partition of the subcontinent.
They have fought two of their three wars over Kashmir.
"As for India, there should be stricter vigil in Kashmir," the Hindustan Times said.
Whatever Pakistan's stand on Kashmir, it was possible that the new administration might move towards beginning dialogue with India, the newspaper said.
